title: Re-gluing a split chair back splat
subtitle: Clamp and re-glue a split or delaminated chair back splat with wood glue and sash cramps
excerpt: How to re-glue a cracked or split central back panel (splat) on a dining or bedroom chair. Covers cleaning the old glue from the split surfaces, applying fresh wood glue, cramping the joint, and allowing a full cure before use.
sourceNotes: Traditional furniture repair practice. Period cabinet-making manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: The central vertical panel of a chair back, running from the top rail to the seat rail. In traditional furniture the splat is a flat or shaped piece of solid hardwood, tenoned or mortised into the top and bottom rails. Victorian and Edwardian chairs commonly use splats of mahogany, walnut, or oak. Splits occur along the grain, usually from the top or bottom mortise upward.

content.text: splits along the grain under lateral stress or from drying shrinkage. The repair is to clean the old glue from the split faces, apply fresh PVA, close the joint under clamping pressure, and allow a full 24-hour cure. The joint is as strong as the original wood once cured correctly.
Assess and open the split if needed

Examine the split with a torch. If the split faces are clean wood, proceed to cleaning. If old glue is visible on the split faces, gently lever the split open slightly with the chisel to expose the full glue line, clean out the old glue, and allow the joint to close again. Do not force the split further than it naturally wants to go: solid wood rarely splits at a right angle and forcing the split can extend it.

Remove all traces of old glue from both faces of the split. Old hide glue (the standard original adhesive on pre-1950 furniture) can be softened by working a cloth dampened with warm water along the split, then scraping off with the flat face of the chisel. Old PVA cannot be softened with water; use fine sandpaper or the chisel to abrade it off. The surfaces must be clean bare wood for PVA to bond to.
Apply glue and cramp the joint

Apply a thin even coat of PVA wood glue to both surfaces of the split. Close the joint by hand, squeezing out any excess glue. Apply clamping pressure across the joint using a sash cramp or a band cramp set to the width of the splat. The cramp should close the joint fully and squeeze a small bead of glue out along the split line. Wipe the excess glue away with a damp cloth before it dries. Pad the cramp jaws with scrap wood to protect the splat face.

Leave the cramp in place for 24 hours at room temperature. PVA reaches its full bond strength in 24 hours; removing the cramp early gives a weaker joint. Once the cramp is removed, use 240-grit sandpaper on the sanding block to smooth any glue squeeze-out along the joint line. Apply a matching wax finish or furniture oil to blend the repair into the surrounding surface.

attrs.symptom: Split reopens within a few weeks of the repair
attrs.cause: Old glue was not fully removed from the joint faces, preventing PVA adhesion.
attrs.fix: The joint must be re-opened, old glue stripped completely, and re-glued. If hide glue is present from the original construction, use fresh hide glue for the repair: it bonds to old hide glue better than PVA.

attrs.symptom: Splat surfaces do not close fully under clamping
attrs.cause: The split faces are not exactly matching (wood has compressed or warped at the split edge).
attrs.fix: Pare the faces lightly with the chisel until they mate cleanly. A thin wedge of matching wood can be glued into a wide gap to fill it before the main gluing.
